entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 16 1Co 16:1-24 . Directions as to the Collection for the Judean Christians: Paul's Future Plans: He Commends to Them Timothy, Apollos, &C. Salutations and Conclusions. 1. collection for the saints-- at Jerusalem ( Ro 15:26 ) and in Judea ( Ac 11:29 , 30 ; 24:17 ; compare 2Co 8:4 ; 9:1 , 12 ). He says "saints" rather than "the poor," to remind the Corinthians that in giving, it is to the Lord's people, their own brethren in the faith. Towards the close of the national existence of the Jews, Judea and Jerusalem were harassed with various troubles, which in part affected the Jewish Christians. The community of goods which existed among them for a time gave temporary relief but tended ultimately to impoverish all by paralyzing individual exertion ( Ac 2:44 ), and hence was soon discontinued. A beautiful fruit of grace it was, that he who had by persecutions robbed many of their all ( Ac 26:10 ), should become the foremost in exertions for their relief. as I have given-- rather, "gave order," namely, during my journey through Galatia, that mentioned in Ac 18:23 . The churches of Galatia and Phrygia were the last which Paul visited before writing this Epistle. He was now at Ephesus, and came thither immediately from visiting them ( Ac 18:23 ; 19:1 ). That he had not been silent in Galatia on contributions for the poor, appears from the hint let fall in his Epistle to that church ( Ga 2:10 ): an undesigned coincidence and mark of genuineness [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ]. He proposes the Galatians as an example to the Corinthians, the Corinthians to the Macedonians, the Corinthians and Macedonians to the Romans ( Ro 15:26 , 27 ; 2Co 9:2 ). There is great force in example.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17147"/><div sID="gen33986" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17147"/><hi type="bold">2. first day of ... week--</hi>already kept sacred by Christians as the day of the Lord's resurrection, the beginning day both of the physical and of the new spiritual creations: it gradually superseded the Jewish sabbath on the seventh day (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.22-Ps.118.24">Psa 118:22-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.19">Joh 20:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.20.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.7">Ac 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>). So the beginning of the year was changed from autumn to spring when Israel was brought out of Egypt. Three annual feasts, all typical of Christian truths, were directed to be kept on the first day of the week: the feast of the wave offering of the first sheaf, answering to the Lord's resurrection; Pentecost, or the feast of weeks, typical of the fruits of the resurrection in the Christian Church (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.11">Le 23:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.16">15, 16</reference>, 36); the feast of tabernacles at harvest, typical of the ingathering of the full number of the elect from one end of heaven to the other. Easter was directed to be kept as a holy sabbath (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.16">Ex 12:16</reference>). The Christian Sabbath commemorates the respective works of the Three Persons of the Triune God--creation, redemption (the resurrection), and sanctification (on Pentecost the Holy Ghost being poured out). Jesus came to fulfil the Spirit of the Law, not to cancel it, or to lower its standard. The primary object of the sabbath is holiness, not merely rest: "Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day." Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Ge 2:3</reference>, "God blessed and sanctified it, because ... in it He had rested," &c. The word "Remember" implies that it was in existence before the giving of the law from Sinai, and refers to its institution in Paradise (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.16.22">Ex 16:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.26">23, 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.30">30</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17148"/><div sID="gen33992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17148"/><hi type="bold">3. approve by your letters--</hi>rather translate, "Whomsoever ye shall approve, them will I send with letters": namely, letters to several persons at Jerusalem, which would be their credentials. There could be no need of letters from them before Paul's coming, if the persons recommended were not to be sent off before it. Literally, "by letters"; an abbreviated expression for "I will send, recommending them by letters" [Grotius]. If English Version be retained, the sense will be, "When I come, I will send those whom by your letters, then to be given them, ye shall approve." But the antithesis (opposition or contrast) to Paul himself (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.4">1Co 16:4</reference>) favors Grotius' view. So "by" means with (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.27">Ro 2:27</reference>); and the Greek for "by" is translated, with (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">2Co 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen33992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33993" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">liberality--</hi>literally, gracious or free gift (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.4">2Co 8:4</reference>). <div eID="gen33993" type="x-p"/>

His first intention had been (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15">2Co 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>) to pass through them (Corinth) to Macedonia, and again return to them from Macedonia, and so to Judea; this he had announced in the lost epistle (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.9">1Co 5:9</reference>); now having laid aside this intention (for which he was charged with levity, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.17">2Co 1:17</reference>, &c., whereas it was through lenity, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.23">2Co 1:23</reference>; 2:1), he announces his second plan of "not seeing them now by the way," but "passing through Macedonia" first on his way to them, and then "tarrying a while," and even "abiding and wintering with them."<div eID="gen33996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for I do pass--</hi>as much as to say, "This is what I at last resolve upon" (not as the erroneous subscription of the Epistle represents it, as if he was THEN at Philippi, on his way through Macedonia); implying that there had been some previous communication upon the subject of the journey, and also that there had been some indecisiveness in the apostle's plan [Paley]. In accordance with his second plan, we find him in Macedonia when Second Corinthians was written (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">2Co 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.1">8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.4">4</reference>), and on his way to Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">2Co 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.1">13:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.20.1">Ac 20:1</reference>, 2). "Pass through" is opposed to "abide" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.6">1Co 16:6</reference>). He was not yet in Macedonia (as <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.8">1Co 16:8</reference> shows), but at Ephesus; but he was thinking of passing through it (not abiding as he purposed to do at Corinth). <div eID="gen33997" type="x-p"/>

Now--</hi>rather, "But." Therefore Timothy was not the bearer of the Epistle; for it would not then be said, "IF Timothy come." He must therefore have been sent by Paul from Ephesus before this Epistle was written, to accord with <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17-1Cor.4.19">1Co 4:17-19</reference>; and yet the passage here implies that Paul did not expect him to arrive at Corinth till after the letter was received. He tells them how to treat him "if" he should arrive. <reference osisRef="Acts.19.21">Ac 19:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">22</reference> clears up the difficulty: Timothy, when sent from Ephesus, where this Epistle was written, did not proceed direct to Corinth, but went first to Macedonia; thus though sent before the letter, he might not reach Corinth till after it was received in that city. The undesigned coincidence between the Epistle and the history, and the clearing up of the meaning of the former (which does not mention the journey to Macedonia at all) by the latter, is a sure mark of genuineness [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ]. It is not certain that Timothy actually reached Corinth; for in <reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">Ac 19:22</reference> only Macedonia is mentioned; but it does not follow that though Macedonia was the immediate object of his mission, Corinth was not the ultimate object. The "IF Timothy come," implies uncertainty. <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference> represents him with Paul in Macedonia; and <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">2Co 12:18</reference>, speaking of Titus and others sent to Corinth, does not mention Timothy, which it would have probably done, had one so closely connected with the apostle as Timothy was, stayed as his delegate at Corinth. But Titus was sent directly to Corinth, so as to arrive there before Timothy could by the route through Macedonia. His youth would add to this feeling, as well as his country, Lystra, likely to be despised in refined Corinth. <div eID="gen34008" type="x-p"/>
